claim: Gregarious female locusts display more synchronous sexual maturation than solitarious females.
source: The curve of the first oviposition time of gregarious females was much narrower than that of solitarious females (60% decrease in the standard deviation [SD], Figure 1A), implying that the first reproductive cycle was more consistent among gregarious female individuals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing 60% decrease in standard deviation of first oviposition time in gregarious vs solitarious females, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Gregarious female locusts display more synchronous sexual maturation than olfactory deficiency mutants.
source: The best-fit normal curve of the first oviposition date was much wider in Orco-/- females than in wild-type (WT) females, when they were reared together with gregarious males (with 63% increase in the SD, Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing 63% increase in standard deviation of first oviposition date in Orco-/- females compared to wild-type females, with reference to Figure 1G.

claim: Gregarious female adults display more uniform and rapid oocyte development patterns than solitarious females after 4 days post adult eclosion.
source: Gregarious female adults displayed more uniform and rapid patterns than that of solitarious females after 4 days post adult eclosion (PAE 4 days) (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of terminal oocyte development with reference to Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only the presence of gregarious male adults can stimulate sexual maturation synchrony of female adults.
source: We found that the maturation synchrony of terminal oocytes of females was significantly retarded by the removal of male adults in gregarious phase (Figure 1C). However, raised with either solitarious female or male did not affect sexual maturation of solitarious females (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that removal of gregarious males retards female maturation synchrony (Figure 1C), while solitarious males or females have no effect (Figure 1D).

claim: Odor blends from gregarious male adults significantly advance the maturation synchrony of gregarious females and solitarious females.
source: The exposure of odor blends from gregarious male adults significantly advanced the maturation synchrony of gregarious females and solitarious females, whereas no effects were observed when exposed to the background air, female odors, or odors from solitarious males (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that odor blends from gregarious males advance female maturation, while other odor sources do not, with reference to Figures 1E, 1F, and supplementary figures.

claim: Olfactory signals from gregarious male adults are essential for triggering the synchrony of female sexual maturation in migratory locusts.
source: Thus, olfactory signals from gregarious male adults are essential for triggering the synchrony of female sexual maturation in migratory locusts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing that Orco-/- females have less synchronous maturation when exposed to gregarious males or their odors (Figure 1H, I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, F).

claim: Five compounds display considerably higher abundance in gregarious male adults compared to gregarious female adults and solitarious male adults after PAE 4 days: PAN, guaicol, 4-vinylanisole, vertrole, and anisole.
source: After PAE 4 days, only five compounds displayed considerably higher abundance in gregarious male adults, compared to that released by gregarious female adults and solitarious male adults, which showed no accelerating effects on female sexual maturation synchrony. Thus, these five kinds of gregarious male adult-abundant volatiles, including PAN, guaicol, 4-vinylanisole (4-VA), vertrole, and anisole (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), might serve as candidate pheromones for female maturation acceleration.
evidence: Supported by chemical analysis data comparing volatile emissions across different locust groups, with reference to Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 4-vinylanisole (4-VA) is the key compound that induces female sexual maturation synchrony.
source: Only the omission of 4-VA, but not other four compounds, from the full blend lost the accelerating effects on sexual maturation synchrony of gregarious females (Figure 2B). Moreover, the exposure to 4-VA can induce similar effects on female sexual maturation synchrony to the full blend (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that only removal of 4-VA from the blend eliminates the maturation-accelerating effect, and 4-VA alone reproduces the full blend effect, with reference to Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The accelerating effects of 4-VA on maturation synchrony display a dose-threshold pattern, with an effective concentration more than 100 ng.
source: In addition, the accelerating effects of 4-VA on maturation synchrony displayed a dose-threshold pattern, with an effective concentration more than 100 ng (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by dose-response experimental data with reference to Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The synchronous effects of 4-VA completely disappear in Or35-/- females.
source: Moreover, the synchronous effects of 4-VA completely disappeared in Or35-/- females (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing 4-VA effects on wild-type versus Or35-/- females, with reference to Figure 2G.

claim: Or35-/- females have a wider distribution of first oviposition date compared to wild-type females (52% increase in standard deviation).
source: Compared to WT females, the best-fit normal curve of the first oviposition date of Or35-/- females was much wider (52% increase in the SD, Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing 52% increase in standard deviation of first oviposition date in Or35-/- females, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Female maturation synchrony is significantly enhanced only when young females are treated by 4-VA at PAE 3–4 days, but not at PAE 1–2 days or PAE 5–6 days.
source: We found that female maturation synchrony was significantly enhanced only when young females were treated by 4-VA at PAE 3–4 days, while did not change at PAE 1–2 days or PAE 5–6 days, indicating the time window of 4-VA action on sexual maturation of females (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential effects of 4-VA treatment at different developmental stages, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The maturation synchrony of females is significantly enhanced by gregarious males aged at PAE 3–4 days and PAE 5–6 days.
source: Moreover, we compared the effects of gregarious males with different ages on female maturation. The maturation synchrony of females was significantly enhanced by gregarious males aged at PAE 3–4 days and PAE 5–6 days (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which could release more 4-VA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing effects of different-aged males on female maturation, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rearing together with the fifth instar of gregarious males and male adults aged at PAE 1–2 days does not significantly affect the maturation synchrony of gregarious female adults.
source: By contrast, rearing together with the fifth instar of gregarious males and male adults aged at PAE 1–2 days did not significantly affect the maturation synchrony of gregarious female adults (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no effect of younger males on female maturation synchrony, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no difference in EAG and SSR responses of females to 4-VA among the ages of PAE 2 days, PAE 4 days, and PAE 6 days.
source: However, there was no difference of EAG and SSRs of females among the ages of PAE 2 days, PAE 4 days, and PAE 6 days, although LmigOr35 expression levels were dynamic during ovary development (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing consistent EAG and SSR responses across different developmental stages, with reference to Figure 3B and supplementary figures.

claim: Peripheral olfactory perception is not involved in the time window effects of 4-VA.
source: These results suggested that peripheral olfactory perception may not be involved in the time window effects of 4-VA.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that EAG and SSR responses do not vary across developmental stages despite differential 4-VA effects.

claim: Gene expression profiles in CC-CA significantly change upon 4-VA treatment, with 290 differentially expressed genes.
source: Notably, gene expression profiles in CC-CA significantly changed upon 4-VA treatment, with 290 DEGs, much more than that in the brain (89 DEGs) (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 5), implying the molecular and physiological activities in CC-CA might be remarkably affected by 4-VA stimuli.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing 290 differentially expressed genes in CC-CA upon 4-VA treatment, with reference to Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: A series of differentially expressed genes in CC-CA involved in juvenile hormone metabolism are enriched upon 4-VA treatment.
source: Moreover, a series of DEGs of CC-CA involved in juvenile hormone (JH) metabolism were enriched. There was significantly higher expression of genes related to JH synthesis but lower expression of genes associated with JH degradation (Figure 3C and D and Figure 3—figure supplement 6 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing enrichment of JH metabolism-related genes with differential expression patterns, with reference to Figures 3C, 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 6, and Supplementary file 1.

claim: JH titer is significantly elevated by 4-VA exposure in females aged at PAE 3–4 days, but not at PAE 1–2 days or PAE 5–6 days.
source: As expected, the JH titer was significantly elicited by 4-VA exposure in females aged at PAE 3–4 days, rather than PAE 1–2 days or PAE 5–6 days (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by JH titer measurements showing stage-specific elevation upon 4-VA exposure, with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: The expression levels of vitellogenin (Vg) are prominently increased in fat body and ovary of females aged at PAE 3–4 days upon 4-VA stimuli.
source: Similarly, the expression levels of vitellogenin (Vg), a key downstream component of JH signaling triggering ovary development in locusts (Song et al., 2014), were prominently increased in fat body and ovary of females aged at PAE 3–4 days upon 4-VA stimuli (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and Western blot data showing increased Vg expression in fat body and ovary upon 4-VA treatment at PAE 3-4 days, with reference to Figures 3F-H and citation to Song et al., 2014.

claim: JH titer does not significantly change in Or35-/- females exposed to 4-VA, in contrast to over twofold increase in wild-type females.
source: By comparison, JH titer did not significantly change in Or35-/- females exposed to 4-VA, contrast to over twofold increase in WT females (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by JH titer measurements comparing wild-type and Or35-/- females upon 4-VA exposure, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Methoprene-injected Or35-/- females display more uniform sexual maturation.
source: Methoprene-injected Or35-/- females displayed more uniform sexual maturation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from JH analog rescue experiments, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: The expression levels of Vg in fat body and ovary significantly increase in methoprene-injected Or35-/- females.
source: Meanwhile, the expression levels of Vg in fat body and ovary significantly increased in methoprene-injected Or35-/- females (Figure 4E and F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and Western blot data from JH analog rescue experiments, with reference to Figures 4E, 4F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibition of JH synthesis by destroying CA using precocene I blocks the 4-VA-accelerated female sexual maturation and Vg expression.
source: Results of rescue experiments on WT females indicated that inhibition of JH synthesis by destroying CA using precocene I blocked the 4-VA-accelarated female sexual maturation and Vg expression, which could be recovered by JH III application after precocene treatment (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from CA ablation and JH rescue experiments, with reference to Figures 4G-I.

claim: The JH/Vg signaling pathway mediates the time-dependent accelerating effects of 4-VA on sexual maturation synchrony in female locusts.
source: These results provide clear evidence that the JH/Vg signaling pathway can mediate the time-dependent accelerating effects of 4-VA on sexual maturation synchrony in female locusts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence including JH titer measurements, Vg expression analysis, and rescue experiments.

claim: Gene expression profiles of fat body display more remarkable changes in female adults exposed to 4-VA at PAE 3–4 days (1700 DEGs) than at PAE 1–2 days (505 DEGs) and at PAE 5–6 days (582 DEGs).
source: Through RNA-seq, we verified that the gene expression profiles of fat body displayed more remarkable changes in female adults exposed to 4-VA at PAE 3–4 days (1700 differentially expressed genes [DEGs]) than those at PAE 1–2 days (505 DEGs) and at PAE 5–6 days (582 DEGs) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data comparing number of differentially expressed genes across different developmental stages, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genes related to energy metabolism are significantly activated by 4-VA treatment at PAE 3–4 days.
source: Notably, genes related to energy metabolism, such as retinol metabolism, glycerolipid metabolism, pyruvate metabolism, as well as fatty acid biosynthesis, which play essential roles in ovary development, were significantly activated by 4-VA treatment at PAE 3–4 days (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by KEGG enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: PAE 3–4 days is a critical time window for 4-VA-induced acceleration of female sexual maturation.
source: Thus, PAE 3–4 days should be a critical time window for 4-VA-induced acceleration of female sexual maturation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including oocyte development, gene expression profiles, JH titer, and Vg expression data.

claim: 4-VA acts as both a primer pheromone and a releaser pheromone in locusts.
source: Thus, a dual role of 4-VA, including both primer and releaser pheromones, could be proposed in triggering the formation of locust swarms.
evidence: Inferred from current study showing primer pheromone effects on maturation and previous studies showing releaser pheromone effects on attraction behavior.

claim: 4-VA is mainly released by gregarious nymphs and male adults.
source: Earlier, we have demonstrated that 4-VA is mainly released by gregarious nymphs and male adults (Wei et al., 2017) and can induce strong attraction behavior of both gregarious and solitarious phases (Guo et al., 2020), indicating its releaser pheromone role in in keeping locust individuals living together.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Wei et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2020).

claim: 4-VA can induce strong attraction behavior of both gregarious and solitarious phases.
source: Earlier, we have demonstrated that 4-VA is mainly released by gregarious nymphs and male adults (Wei et al., 2017) and can induce strong attraction behavior of both gregarious and solitarious phases (Guo et al., 2020), indicating its releaser pheromone role in in keeping locust individuals living together.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Guo et al., 2020).

claim: Reproductive synchrony generally occurs in various group-living animals.
source: Reproductive synchrony generally occurs in various group-living animals.
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge about reproductive synchrony in group-living animals.

claim: Reproductive synchrony may offer adaptive advantages for group-living species, such as predation swamping and inbreeding avoidance.
source: Reproductive synchrony may offer adaptive advantages for group-living species, such as predation swamping and inbreeding avoidance (Janzen, 1971).
evidence: Supported by citation to Janzen, 1971.

claim: Social interaction is considerably critical for triggering reproductive synchrony of individuals in group-living species.
source: Social interaction is considerably critical for triggering reproductive synchrony of individuals in group-living species (French and Stribley, 1985; Ims and Steen, 1990; Jovani and Grimm, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to French and Stribley, 1985; Ims and Steen, 1990; Jovani and Grimm, 2008.

claim: The Whitten effect is induced by the presence of males in rodents, ewes, and monkey.
source: A well-known example is the Whitten effect which is induced by the presence of males in rodents, ewes, and monkey (Vandenbergh, 1967; Cahill et al., 1974; Gattermann et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vandenbergh, 1967; Cahill et al., 1974; Gattermann et al., 2002.

claim: Various kinds of signals, odors, touch, or voice can act as social clues to underpin synchronization with reproduction.
source: Various kinds of signals, odors, touch, or voice can act as social clues to underpin synchronization with reproduction (Rekwot et al., 2001; Kobayashi et al., 2002; Noguera and Velando, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rekwot et al., 2001; Kobayashi et al., 2002; Noguera and Velando, 2019.

claim: Endo-signals, such as hormone release, gene expression, and epigenetic modification, have been suggested to be involved in reproductive synchronization processes.
source: Endo-signals, such as hormone release, gene expression, and epigenetic modification, have also been suggested to be involved in these interaction processes (Engel et al., 2016; Noguera and Velando, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engel et al., 2016; Noguera and Velando, 2019.

claim: Gregarious locusts display much higher synchrony in physiological and behavioral events compared to solitarious conspecifics.
source: Gregarious locusts, compared to solitarious conspecifics, show much higher synchrony in physiological and behavioral events, such as egg hatching and sexual maturation, as well as synchronous feeding and marching behaviors (Norris, 1954; Uvarov, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citations to Norris, 1954; Uvarov, 1977.

claim: Reproductive synchrony in gregarious locusts provides benefits such as more favorable microenvironment, lower risk of predation, efficient foraging, and more encounters with mates.
source: Reproductive synchrony in gregarious locusts provides benefits for individuals in several aspects, such as more favorable microenvironment, lower risk of predation, efficiently forging, as well as more encounters with mates, therefore ensures high-density conditions for the next generation, and is essential for maintenance of locust swarm (Beekman et al., 2008, Maeno et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beekman et al., 2008, Maeno et al., 2021.

claim: Vibratory stimulus, maternal microRNAs, and SNARE protein play important roles in the egg-hatching synchrony of gregarious locusts.
source: Some sort of vibratory stimulus, maternal microRNAs, and SNARE protein play important roles in the egg-hatching synchrony of gregarious locusts (Chen et al., 2015; He et al., 2016; Nishide and Tanaka, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015; He et al., 2016; Nishide and Tanaka, 2016.

claim: The presence of mature male adults has effectively accelerating effects on synchrony of sexual maturation of immature male and female conspecifics in Schistocerca gregaria and Locusta migratoria.
source: It has been revealed that the presence of mature male adults has effectively accelerating effects on synchrony of sexual maturation of immature male and female conspecifics in two locust species, Schistocerca gregaria and Locusta migratoria (Norris, 1952; Loher, 1997; Guo and Xia, 1964; Norris and Richards, 1964).
evidence: Supported by citations to Norris, 1952; Loher, 1997; Guo and Xia, 1964; Norris and Richards, 1964.

claim: Four volatile pheromones (benzaldehyde, veratrole, phenylacetonitrile, and 4-vinylveratrole) have significantly stimulatory effects on sexual maturation of male adults in the desert locust, with PAN having the most pronounced effect.
source: Four volatile pheromones (benzaldehyde, veratrole, phenylacetonitrile [PAN], and 4-vinylveratrole) have significantly stimulatory effects on sexual maturation of male adults, with PAN having the most pronounced effect (Mahamat et al., 1993; Assad et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mahamat et al., 1993; Assad et al., 1997.

claim: Vitellogenin (Vg) is a key downstream component of JH signaling triggering ovary development in locusts.
source: Similarly, the expression levels of vitellogenin (Vg), a key downstream component of JH signaling triggering ovary development in locusts (Song et al., 2014), were prominently increased in fat body and ovary of females aged at PAE 3–4 days upon 4-VA stimuli (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2014.

claim: JH signaling pathway presents as the major gonadotropin modulating Vg biosynthesis in the fat body and its uptake by the growing oocytes in the migratory locust.
source: This finding is consistent with the role of JH as the major gonadotropin modulating Vg biosynthesis in the fat body and its uptake by the growing oocytes in the migratory locust (Jindra et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2014; Song et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jindra et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2014; Song et al., 2014.

claim: The release of the maturation-accelerating pheromone by adult males is under the control of CA.
source: Interesting, it has been suggested that the release of the maturation-accelerating pheromone by adult males is under the control of CA (Loher, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Loher, 1997.

claim: JH signaling plays central roles in mediating the effects of social interactions on reproduction in different kinds of insect species.
source: Extensive studies have established the central roles of JH signaling in mediating the effects of social interactions on reproduction in different kinds of insect species, including eusocial insects (Robinson and Vargo, 1997; Korb, 2015), the burying beetle, Nicrophorus vespilloides (Engel et al., 2016), the German cockroach, Blattella germanica (Uzsák and Schal, 2012), and so on.
evidence: Supported by citations to Robinson and Vargo, 1997; Korb, 2015; Engel et al., 2016; Uzsák and Schal, 2012.

claim: Interaction between social clues and internal hormonal signals that coordinates ovary development is common among group-living vertebrates.
source: Such an interaction between social clues and internal hormonal signals that coordinates ovary development is also common among group-living vertebrates (Drickamer, 1977; McClintock, 1978; Berger, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Drickamer, 1977; McClintock, 1978; Berger, 1992.

claim: JH titers, Vg expression, and the size of terminal oocytes dramatically increase at PAE 3–4 days in female locusts.
source: It has been shown that JH titers, Vg expression, the size of terminal oocytes, dramatically increased at PAE 3–4 days, implies the PAE 3–4 days is an essential time window for JH-regulated ovary development in female locusts (Luo et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luo et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018.

claim: In insects, it is very common for males to mature earlier than females.
source: In insects, it is very common for males to mature earlier than females (Alonzo, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alonzo, 2013.

claim: In the locust, male adults display earlier sexual maturation for several days, compared to females.
source: In the locust, male adults also display earlier sexual maturation for several days, compared to females.
evidence: Statement of observed pattern in locusts, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: Peripheral and central neural sensitivity to olfactory clues vary with developmental stages or physiological statuses.
source: Peripheral and central neural sensitivity to olfactory clues have been demonstrated to vary with developmental stages or physiological statuses (Guo et al., 2011; Gadenne et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guo et al., 2011; Gadenne et al., 2016.

claim: Orco-/- mutants display significant olfactory deficiency.
source: To further explore the roles of olfactory cues in females' sexual maturation process, we examined the performance of loss-of-function mutants of olfactory receptor co-receptor gene (Orco-/-) established by CRISPR/Cas9, which display significant olfactory deficiency (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: Or35-/- females cannot sense 4-VA.
source: We further examined the performance of Or35-/- females that cannot sense 4-VA (Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2020.

claim: The sexual maturation in Or35-/- females is more uneven than that of WT females when they are reared together with gregarious males.
source: The sexual maturation in Or35-/- females was more uneven than that of WT females when they were reared together with gregarious males (Figure 2F) or exposed to the odors of gregarious males (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing sexual maturation patterns in Or35-/- versus WT females, with reference to Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Gene expression profiles in fat body tissue correlate tightly with the sexual maturation of female locusts.
source: Gene expression profiles in fat body tissue have been demonstrated to correlate tightly with the sexual maturation of female locusts (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2014.

claim: The release of 4-VA by gregarious males continuously increases after adult eclosion, with maximal 4-VA release at PAE 8 days.
source: We find that the release of 4-VA by gregarious males continuously increased after adult eclosion, with maximal 4-VA release at PAE 8 days.
evidence: Inferred from the volatile emission dynamics data presented in the study.

claim: In given locust population, individuals successively emerge to adults in a couple of days.
source: In given locust population, individuals successively emerge to adults in a couple of days.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of locust population dynamics.

claim: Age-dependent increase in 4-VA release in gregarious male adults presents a persistent stimulus for less-developed young female adults, maximizing maturation synchrony of female locusts.
source: Therefore, age-dependent increase in 4-VA release in gregarious male adults presents a persistent stimulus for less-developed young female adults, and thus maximizes maturation synchrony of female locusts, which could reduce male competitions for mate selection.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of 4-VA release dynamics and time-window effects on female maturation.

claim: 4-VA has been identified in the volatiles released by male adults of Schistocerca gregaria.
source: Recently, 4-VA has been identified in the volatiles released by male adults of S. gregaria (Torto et al., 2021), whether this volatile has maturation-accelerating effect in this locust species needs further validation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Torto et al., 2021.

claim: The fifth nymphs have been shown to display inhibiting effects on male maturation in S. gregaria.
source: In fact, the fifth nymphs have been shown to display inhibiting effects on male maturation in S. gregaria (Assad et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Assad et al., 1997.

claim: The mechanisms underlying pheromone-mediated sexual maturation may differ between different locust species.
source: Therefore, the mechanisms underlying pheromone-mediated sexual maturation may differ between different locust species.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that fifth nymphs have different effects on maturation in different locust species.

claim: Extremely high energy cost for female reproduction could restrict migration to pre-, post-, or inter-oviposition period in locusts.
source: Extremely high energy cost for female reproduction could restrict migration to pre-, post-, or inter-oviposition period in locusts, thus have crucial effects on collective movement of local populations (Min et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Min et al., 2004.

claim: Young female adults reared with older gregarious male adults show faster and more synchronous sexual maturation in the migratory locust.
source: We here demonstrated that young female adults reared with older gregarious male adults show faster and more synchronous sexual maturation in the migratory locust, supporting the accelerate role of crowding in sexual maturation of females (Guo and Xia, 1964; Norris and Richards, 1964).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the current study and citations to Guo and Xia, 1964; Norris and Richards, 1964.

claim: Young adults of both sexes lived in gregarious conditions prefer more synchronous maturation than individuals reared in solitary.
source: Together with the accelerating effects on immature male sexual maturation induced by older gregarious male adults reported previously (Torto et al., 1994; Mahamat et al., 2011), young adults of both sexes lived in gregarious conditions prefer more synchronous maturation than individuals reared in solitary.
evidence: Inferred from current study results combined with citations to Torto et al., 1994; Mahamat et al., 2011.

claim: The consistent maturation in both sexes will greatly reduce intra- and inter-sexes competitions for mate selection and thus ensures reproductive synchronous in whole locust populations.
source: The consistent maturation in both sexes will greatly reduce intra- and inter-sexes competitions for mate selection and thus ensures reproductive synchronous in whole locust populations.
evidence: Inferred from the observed patterns of maturation synchrony in both sexes.

claim: There might exist a sex-dependent action modes of maturation-accelerating pheromones: multi-component pheromones for males and single active component for females.
source: Thus, there might exist a sex-dependent action modes of maturation-accelerating pheromones: multi-component pheromones for males and single active component for females, possibly due to different selective pressures between two sexes in response to social interaction.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the observation that four volatiles affect male maturation while only 4-VA affects female maturation.

claim: It is likely an effective and optimized strategy of group-living animals to use a single chemical pheromone to elicit both behavioral and endocrine responses in conspecifics.
source: It is likely an effective and optimized strategy of group-living animals to use a single chemical pheromone to elicit both behavioral and endocrine responses in conspecifics (Rekwot et al., 2001).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to Rekwot et al., 2001.

claim: The action of 4-VA displays a remarkable context-dependent manner, such as phase-, sex-, dose-, and time-dependent.
source: The action of 4-VA displays a remarkable context-dependent manner, such as phase-, sex-, dose-, and time-dependent, reflecting physiological adaption of locusts to the highly dynamic nature of population density.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations showing different effects of 4-VA under different conditions.

claim: Only gregarious males aged after PAE 3 days have the accelerating effects on female maturation synchrony.
source: We find that only gregarious males aged after PAE 3 days have the accelerating effects on female maturation synchrony, which may be attributed to their significantly increased 4-VA content during adult development.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing age-dependent effects of males on female maturation.

claim: The accelerating effects on female maturation synchrony induced by gregarious male adults may depend largely on 4-VA content they released.
source: Thus, the accelerating effects on female maturation synchrony induced by gregarious male adults may depend largely on 4-VA content they released.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only older males with higher 4-VA content have accelerating effects.

claim: The ineffectiveness of the fifth nymphs and females in maturation acceleration of female adults may be due to their low 4-VA content under efficient threshold.
source: Although gregarious nymphs (the fifth instar) and female adults can release relatively small amount of 4-VA (Wei et al., 2017), they did not promote female maturation based on our current results. Thus, the accelerating effects on female maturation synchrony induced by gregarious male adults may depend largely on 4-VA content they released. The ineffectiveness of the fifth nymphs and females in maturation acceleration of female adults may due to their low 4-VA content under efficient threshold.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations combined with citation to Wei et al., 2017.

claim: There should be a complex feedback interaction between 4-VA and JH signaling pathway.
source: Thus, there should be a complex feedback interaction between 4-VA and JH signaling pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both 4-VA affects JH synthesis and JH affects pheromone release.

claim: Signaling factors responsible for JH synthesis might be turned on specifically at Mid-PAE of female locusts upon 4-VA stimuli, such as GPCRs and transcription factors.
source: A possible explanation is that signaling factors responsible for JH synthesis might be turned on specifically at Mid-PAE of female locusts upon 4-VA stimuli, such as GPCRs and transcription factors (Bendena et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citation to Bendena et al., 2020.

claim: The central nerve system pathway might be involved in 4-VA effects through mechanisms such as neurotransmitter release or post-transcription regulation.

evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to Nouzova et al., 2018.

claim: The migratory locust displays synchronous maturation and oviposition when it forms huge swarms.

claim: 4-VA promotes the synchrony of sexual maturation in female locusts through a 'catch-up' strategy.
source: Our results highlight a 'catch-up' strategy by which gregarious females synchronize their oocyte maturation and oviposition by time-dependent endocrinal response to 4-vinylanisole, and provide insight into reproductive synchrony induced by olfactory signal released by heterosexual conspecifics in a given group.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that 4-VA mainly accelerates maturation of less-developed females.

claim: 4-VA mainly accelerates oocyte maturation of young females aged at middle developmental stages (3–4 days post adult eclosion).
source: Interestingly, 4-vinylanisole displayed a time window action by which mainly accelerates oocyte maturation of young females aged at middle developmental stages (3–4 days post adult eclosion).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing stage-specific effects of 4-VA.

claim: Juvenile hormone/vitellogenin pathway mediates female sexual maturation triggered by 4-vinylanisole.
source: We further revealed that juvenile hormone/vitellogenin pathway mediated female sexual maturation triggered by 4-vinylanisole.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including JH titer measurements, Vg expression analysis, and rescue experiments.
